title: Kaliya

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaliya: the boy went still in the serpent's coils, the village wept on the bank, and Balarama smiled. Where did you take one calm breath before reacting? Day eight hundred ninety-three.

Why does he go still? In the Bhagavata's telling, he isn't overpowered. It describes him lying in the coils for a while, and then it turns the camera to the bank, to his mother and friends and the cows, all of them stricken. Then it turns back to the water. Krishna sees them. He sees what his stillness is doing to the people who love him, and the text says he stays bound, playing the part of a mortal, only for a short time. Then he decides that's enough. Today, the boy gets up.
screen: `WHY DOES HE GO STILL?` → `HE SEES THE GRIEF ON THE BANK.` → `THAT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Krishna makes his body grow. The coils, which were holding a small boy, are suddenly stretched around something they can't contain, and Kaliya has to let go. The serpent rears up, hissing, his eyes burning, his breath smoking with poison, and the two of them circle in the water, Krishna moving around him the way Garuda, the great eagle, circles a snake. Kaliya follows him until he's worn out. And then Krishna does something stranger. He presses down Kaliya's raised hoods, climbs up onto them, and begins to dance. The text treats it as a real performance. Celestial musicians gather. Drums and songs and flowers come down from the sky. And on the stage of the serpent's heads, the boy dances. Whichever hood Kaliya lifts, Krishna's feet come down on it, keeping time. Kaliya thrashes and then weakens. Blood comes from his mouths. His hoods are broken, his pride with them. And at last, exhausted, the serpent turns his mind toward the one dancing on him, and, the text says, remembers the ancient Lord. What Krishna leaves undone matters. He doesn't kill Kaliya. He doesn't strike him with a weapon. The fight becomes a dance, and the dance goes on until the poison in the serpent's pride is gone. In Hindu art and song the scene is known as Kaliya-mardana, the subduing of Kaliya: a small boy, one foot raised, dancing on a cobra's hood.
screen: `HE GROWS, AND THE COILS LET GO.` · `THEY CIRCLE IN THE WATER.` · `HE DANCES ON THE HOODS.` · then, large: `THE SERPENT REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the rhythm of your breath, in and out, like steps in a slow dance. Bring to mind one thing in you that keeps rearing up: a temper, a habit, a hard voice in your head. Don't fight it. Just notice each time it lifts its head, and let your breath come down gently on it, one beat at a time. In. Out. Steady, unhurried, until it settles a little. If you pray, you can offer that struggle in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Kaliya. The serpent whose coils can't hold the growing boy, and whose pride is danced out of him on his own hoods.
Your line: Kaliya. Today, when an old temper or habit rears up, meet it with steady rhythm, not a fight. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Krishna dancing on Kaliya's hoods, Kaliya-mardana, appears in temple sculpture, bronzes, paintings and classical dance, and devotees tell it among the stories of Krishna's childhood in Vraja.
